subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 18 periods = 900 minutes
Total: 18 periods · 15h 0min

periods.activity_title: Locating Objects Using a Reference Point on a Number Line
materials: Chalk or masking tape for floor markings
periods.visual_aids: Number line diagram drawn on board showing origin O, positive direction (right), and negative direction (left)

time_bands.activity: Students stand in a line in the classroom. The teacher marks a spot on the floor as 'O' (the origin). Students are asked: 'How would you describe where each person is standing?' Responses are collected and the idea of needing a reference point emerges from discussion.

The teacher draws a number line on the board with O at centre. Students are given positions (e.g., 3 m to the right, 2 m to the left) and must assign positive or negative values. They then reverse the task: given a signed number, they state the physical location.

In pairs, students invent two scenarios — one where an object is at rest (position does not change over two instants) and one where it is in motion (position changes). They record both scenarios as number-line sketches and write one sentence explaining what 'motion' means based on the pattern they see.

Pairs share their sketches. Class compares rest vs. motion cases and consolidates the definition: an object is in motion if its position with respect to the origin changes with time, at rest if it does not.

Quick individual check: the teacher calls out three positions (e.g., −4 m, 0 m, +6 m) and asks students to mark them on a rough number line and state whether an object moving from −4 m to +6 m is in motion or at rest.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's entry point, so begin by letting students voice their everyday sense of 'position' before formalising it. A common error is treating position as always positive — stress that the sign encodes direction, not quality. If a student places the origin at the left end by habit, use it to show that the choice of origin is arbitrary but must be stated.

periods.activity_title: Comparing Distance and Displacement for a Ball Thrown Upward
materials: Printed or drawn number-line worksheet (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Number line on board showing the vertical path of a ball thrown upward and returning to start

time_bands.activity: The teacher sketches a vertical number line on the board and describes: a ball is thrown upward from position 0 m to +5 m, then falls back to 0 m. Students are asked to predict (a) the total distance travelled and (b) the displacement.

Students individually fill a table (Activity 4.1 format) with columns: start position, end position, total distance, and displacement for three stages — (i) 0 to +5 m, (ii) +5 m back to 0 m, (iii) the full round trip. They use the number line worksheet to trace the path and count metres.

Class discussion: students compare their tables. The teacher draws out the key insight — distance is always positive and accumulates, while displacement depends on initial and final position only. The athlete example (running back and forth) from the chapter is discussed: distance > displacement when direction reverses.

Students write two sentences: one defining distance (scalar, total path length) and one defining displacement (vector-like, net change in position with direction). They swap with a neighbour for peer review against the board definition.
Exit check: teacher poses — 'An object moves 8 m east then 3 m west. State the distance and displacement.' Students write answers on a slip.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that position is measured from an origin, this unit builds directly on that sign convention: displacement inherits its sign from the direction of net change. The most persistent error is students treating displacement as always equal to distance — the round-trip ball scenario is the clearest counter-example to press on. Confirm readiness by checking that students can correctly sign displacements for paths that involve reversal.

periods.activity_title: Calculating Average Speed and Average Velocity from Motion Data
periods.visual_aids: Table on board showing uniform vs. non-uniform motion examples with equal time intervals

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents the two equations: average speed = total distance / time interval (Eq. 4.1) and average velocity = displacement / time interval (Eq. 4.2a–b). A table is drawn on the board contrasting uniform motion (equal distances per equal time interval) with non-uniform motion. Students identify which row is uniform and which is not.

The teacher works through one numerical example on the board: an object travels 12 m in one direction, then 4 m back, in 8 s — students compute both average speed and average velocity step by step, noting the sign convention for direction.

Students work in pairs on the worksheet: three varied scenarios (one uniform, two non-uniform) requiring calculation of average speed and average velocity. At least one scenario has zero displacement (round trip) to distinguish speed from velocity clearly.
Pair-share: two pairs compare answers and resolve any discrepancies. The teacher circulates and targets common errors — particularly sign errors or averaging speeds instead of using total distance.
Teacher consolidates: average velocity is the average rate of change of position with respect to time; it can be zero even when speed is not.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established displacement as a signed quantity, this unit applies that signed quantity in the velocity formula. A frequent error is computing average velocity as the arithmetic mean of two individual velocities instead of displacement divided by time — pose the round-trip case to expose this. Ask students to articulate why average speed and average velocity can have the same numerical value only when the object moves in a single direction without turning.
homework: A cyclist rides 600 m north in 120 s, then 200 m south in 40 s. Calculate (a) average speed and (b) average velocity for the whole journey, using the sign convention that north is positive.

periods.activity_title: Computing Average Acceleration from Velocity Change over Time
periods.visual_aids: Board table from Example 4.3 (bus accelerating then braking) showing velocity values at successive instants

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the definition: average acceleration = change in velocity / time interval (Eq. 4.3a–c). The sign convention is stated: acceleration is in the direction of velocity when speed increases, opposite when speed decreases. Units (m s⁻²) are recorded.

The teacher works through Example 4.3 (bus accelerating then braking) step by step on the board, calculating acceleration for both phases and asking students to interpret the sign of acceleration in each case. Example 4.4 (free fall with g = 9.8 m s⁻²) is then shown as a case of constant acceleration.

Students work individually on the worksheet: three problems involving constant positive acceleration, deceleration (negative acceleration), and one case of constant g. They must state both magnitude and direction (sign) of acceleration in each answer.
Students form groups of three and compare answers, particularly sign conventions. Teacher leads a brief whole-class discussion on any persistent sign errors.
Consolidation: teacher elicits one sentence from the class — 'Acceleration can be opposite to the direction of velocity when…' — to confirm the deceleration concept.

periods.teacher_notes: The definition of velocity as a signed quantity, established in the previous section, is essential scaffolding here — acceleration inherits its sign from the direction of velocity change. Students frequently confuse negative acceleration with slowing down in all cases; the free-fall example is useful to show that downward acceleration (negative by convention) speeds up a falling object. Probe with: 'Can an object have positive velocity and negative acceleration at the same time?' to surface this distinction.
homework: A car's velocity changes from +20 m s⁻¹ to +8 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. Calculate the average acceleration, state its sign, and explain in one sentence what the sign indicates about the relationship between acceleration and velocity.

periods.activity_title: Plotting a Position-Time Graph from Vehicle Data Step by Step
materials: Data table (Table 4.3 from chapter — vehicle position vs. time)
periods.visual_aids: Table 4.3 written on the board; teacher-drawn example of labelled axes with scale markings

time_bands.activity: The teacher models how to set up axes: label X-axis as time (s), Y-axis as position (m), choose a scale that spreads data across the paper, and mark uniform intervals. Students follow on their own graph paper.

Students work through Activity 4.3: they read Table 4.3 values, plot each (time, position) point carefully, and connect the points. The teacher circulates checking scale choice and point placement. Students observe that the result is a straight line.

The teacher displays Table 4.4 (accelerating data from Example 4.5) on the board. Students plot this second data set on the same or a new sheet. They observe that the points do not form a straight line — a curve results. Students compare the two graphs and write one sentence describing the visual difference.

Class discussion: what does a straight line vs. a curve tell us about the motion? Students connect the visual pattern to constant vs. changing velocity from what they know about uniform and non-uniform motion.
Students label their completed graphs with the type of motion each represents (uniform or non-uniform) and keep them for the next activity.

periods.teacher_notes: The mechanics of accurate plotting — scale selection, axis labelling, and uniform spacing — are a genuine procedural skill and deserve full attention here. A common error is choosing a scale that crams all points into one corner; encourage students to compute the range of values before selecting a scale. The two-graph comparison (straight line vs. curve) is the conceptual payoff of this unit and should not be rushed.

periods.activity_title: Reading Position-Time Graph Slopes to Determine Average Velocity
materials: Graph paper with a position-time straight-line graph (students draw fresh or use Period 5 graph)
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn position-time graph on board showing segment AB, construction lines BC and CA forming a right triangle

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a position-time graph on the board with a straight line (constant velocity), a horizontal line (at rest), and a curve (accelerating). Students classify each and explain their reasoning aloud.

Students carry out Activity 4.4: on their position-time graph (straight line), they mark a segment AB, draw vertical line BC and horizontal line CA to form triangle ABC, measure BC (change in position) and CA (change in time), and calculate BC/CA. They compare this ratio to the velocity value they would expect from the original data.

The teacher introduces the formal interpretation: slope of position-time graph = average velocity. Students apply this to two different segments of their graph and compare slopes, then discuss which segment represents higher velocity and why.

Students sketch two position-time lines for two objects on the same axes — one steeper, one shallower — and write a comparison statement: which object has greater velocity and how the slope encodes that.
Exit check: teacher asks — 'What does a line parallel to the time axis tell you about the object's velocity?' Students answer individually in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having plotted graphs in the previous unit, students now extract physical meaning from their shape. The most common error is computing slope as CA/BC (inverted) — reinforce that slope is always rise over run, i.e., change in position over change in time. Ask students to check whether their calculated slope matches the velocity they would compute directly from the data to build confidence in the graphical method.

periods.activity_title: Interpreting Velocity-Time Graph Slopes and Enclosed Areas
periods.visual_aids: Board sketches of velocity-time graphs: horizontal line, positive slope, negative slope, and shaded rectangle/trapezoid for area

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws three velocity-time graphs on the board: (a) horizontal line — constant velocity; (b) straight line with positive slope — constant acceleration; (c) straight line with negative slope — constant deceleration. Students identify and state what each implies about acceleration.

Teacher demonstrates slope calculation using the triangle method (Figs. 4.17d and 4.17e): marks two points, draws vertical and horizontal construction lines, computes change in velocity / change in time. Students replicate this on their worksheet graphs for both a positive-slope and a negative-slope line.

Teacher introduces the area interpretation: the area under a velocity-time graph equals displacement. For a rectangle (constant velocity), students calculate area = base × height = time × velocity = displacement. For a trapezoid (changing velocity, Fig. 4.18b), students apply the trapezoid area formula and confirm with the worked numerical example from the chapter.

Students work in pairs on a short application: given a velocity-time graph with both a constant-velocity phase and an accelerating phase, they calculate acceleration from slope and total displacement from area.
Consolidation: teacher elicits the two key relationships — slope gives acceleration, area gives displacement — as a paired summary written by each student.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have interpreted position-time graphs in terms of slope will find the slope-equals-acceleration relationship here structurally familiar; draw out that analogy explicitly. A frequent error is confusing the area under the graph with the area of the graph paper — stress that area here is computed as a physical product (velocity × time = metres) and has units. The trapezoid case is the conceptually harder step; check that students correctly identify the two parallel sides before computing.
homework: A velocity-time graph shows an object accelerating uniformly from 4 m s⁻¹ to 12 m s⁻¹ over 4 s, then moving at constant 12 m s⁻¹ for 3 s. Calculate (a) the acceleration during the first phase and (b) the total displacement over both phases using areas.

periods.activity_title: Deriving the First Two Kinematic Equations from Definitions and Graphs
periods.section_anchor: 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
periods.visual_aids: Velocity-time graph on board (Fig. 4.19) showing initial velocity u at t=0, final velocity v at time t, with shaded trapezoidal area for displacement

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the velocity-time graph for constant acceleration on the board (Fig. 4.19). Students identify the slope and are guided to write: a = (v − u)/t, rearranged to v = u + at (Eq. 4.4a). Each symbol is named and its unit stated.

Teacher shades the trapezoidal area under the graph (from 0 to t) and asks students to calculate it. They apply the trapezoid area formula: s = ½(u + v)t. Substituting v = u + at into this expression, students derive s = ut + ½at² (Eq. 4.4b) step by step on their notebooks.

Teacher guides the elimination of t between Eq. 4.4a and Eq. 4.4b to derive v² = u² + 2as (Eq. 4.4c). Students record each algebraic step and underline the condition of validity: constant acceleration.

Students apply Eq. 4.4c to Example 4.8 (car decelerating at −4 m s⁻²): they calculate stopping distance for an initial speed, then double the initial speed and recalculate, confirming that stopping distance quadruples. They write a one-sentence conclusion connecting this to road safety.
Quick individual check: teacher calls out a scenario — 'u = 0, a = 2 m s⁻², t = 5 s, find v and s' — students solve using Eq. 4.4a and 4.4b.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivations here rest on the velocity-time graph interpretation developed in the preceding graphical unit — specifically, that slope gives acceleration and area gives displacement. Students often apply kinematic equations without checking the constant-acceleration condition; make it explicit that these equations fail for variable acceleration. The stopping-distance quadrupling result is a powerful motivator — press students to articulate the algebraic reason, not just note the numerical outcome.

periods.activity_title: Applying All Three Kinematic Equations to Solve Motion Problems
periods.section_anchor: 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
materials: Worksheet with four to five kinematic equation problems (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Summary table on board: three equations, five variables (s, t, u, v, a), and the variable absent from each equation

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the summary table on the board — three equations mapped to the variable each one lacks (v = u + at lacks s; s = ut + ½at² lacks v; v² = u² + 2as lacks t). Students practice identifying which equation to use given a set of known variables.

Students work individually on the worksheet problems, which include: (a) finding displacement given u, a, t; (b) finding final velocity given u, a, s; (c) a deceleration problem requiring correct negative sign for a; (d) a free-fall problem with g = 9.8 m s⁻². Students must state the equation chosen and why.
Students form pairs and compare solutions, focusing on equation selection and sign conventions. Pairs identify one problem where they disagreed and prepare to explain it to the class.
Two or three pairs share their disagreement cases. Class resolves each, with teacher redirecting to the constant-acceleration condition and sign rules.
Each student writes one sentence: 'I must check __ before using these equations.' to consolidate the validity condition.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived the three equations in the previous unit, this unit builds fluency with their application under varied given-unknown combinations. The most common error is ignoring the sign of acceleration — particularly in deceleration problems where students write a as a positive number. Probe with: 'How do you know which sign to give a in this problem?' to force explicit reasoning about direction.
homework: A stone is dropped from rest. Using g = 9.8 m s⁻², calculate (a) the velocity after 3 s and (b) the distance fallen in 3 s. State which kinematic equation you used for each part and why.

periods.activity_title: Connecting Kinematic Equations to Graph Shapes for Constant Acceleration
periods.section_anchor: 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn velocity-time graph on board for a constant-acceleration scenario showing the trapezoidal area shaded

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents a scenario: an object starts with u = 2 m s⁻¹ and accelerates at a = 3 m s⁻² for 6 s. Students compute velocity at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 s using v = u + at and record in a table.

Students plot the velocity-time graph from their computed table on graph paper, draw the best-fit straight line, compute its slope, and confirm it matches a = 3 m s⁻². They then shade the area under the line from t = 0 to t = 6 s and compute the area (trapezoid).

Students verify the area equals the displacement computed algebraically using s = ut + ½at². They write a comparison showing that both methods yield the same displacement, identifying this as a coherence check between the equations and the graph.

Discussion: teacher asks — 'If acceleration were zero, what would the velocity-time graph look like, and what would s = ut + ½at² reduce to?' Students respond, connecting the graph shape to a special case of the equation.
Students annotate their completed graph: label slope with acceleration value, label shaded area with displacement value, and note the equation used for each.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit reinforces the coherence between the algebraic equations and the graphical representation — both derived from the same velocity-time relationship. Students who successfully complete the area-equals-s check develop genuine confidence that the equations are not arbitrary formulas but compressed descriptions of the graph. Watch for errors in computing the trapezoid area; confirm students identify the two parallel sides (velocities at t = 0 and t = 6 s) correctly.

periods.activity_title: Historical Problem-Solving: Speed from the Aryabhatiya and Ganitakaumudi
periods.section_anchor: 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
materials: Printed extract or board-written text of the Ganitakaumudi problem

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the historical context: the concept of speed as distance divided by time appears in the Aryabhatiya (5th century CE). The class discusses what it means for a mathematical relationship to appear in a text over 1500 years old.

The Ganitakaumudi problem is read aloud (or displayed). Students work individually or in pairs to identify the known quantities and the unknown, set up the relationship speed = distance / time, and solve the problem, showing all steps.

Students compare their setups and solutions. The teacher facilitates discussion: is the mathematical principle the same as what we use today? Students articulate the continuity between historical and contemporary formulation.

Students write a short justification (3–4 sentences) explaining how the Ganitakaumudi problem is an application of average speed as defined in this chapter, connecting the historical text explicitly to Eq. 4.1.
Class shares one or two justifications and the teacher consolidates the connection between the classical definition and the modern formula.

periods.teacher_notes: The road safety and historical material in the chapter offers a genuine opportunity to show students that the physics of motion is not culturally neutral. Students may initially treat the historical problem as a novelty; push them to write the formal equation explicitly so they see the structural identity. If the Ganitakaumudi text is not in the school's edition, the teacher may use the road safety stopping-distance scenario from the same bridging box as an alternative application context.

periods.activity_title: Introducing Two-Dimensional Motion and Its Everyday Examples
materials: Open space in classroom or corridor
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of a kicked ball's curved path and a satellite's circular orbit contrasted with a straight-line path

time_bands.activity: Teacher gently kicks or rolls a ball across the classroom floor in a straight path, then rolls it along a curved path (deflecting mid-path). Students observe and describe the difference. The teacher asks: 'How many dimensions does each path use?'

Teacher presents the three examples from the chapter — a vehicle overtaking, a kicked ball, a satellite in orbit — on the board. Students classify each as one-dimensional or two-dimensional and give a reason. The definition of motion in a plane (movement in two dimensions) is formalised.

Students brainstorm in pairs: list three real-world motions that are strictly two-dimensional and three that are one-dimensional. They sketch a simple path diagram for each of their two-dimensional examples.
Pairs share their lists. Class discusses borderline cases: is a car on a winding road one- or two-dimensional? Students refine their definitions.
Students write a one-sentence definition of motion in a plane in their own words, then compare with a neighbour and agree on a joint formulation.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's second major domain — two-dimensional motion — and the key conceptual step is recognising that an object's path can require two coordinates to describe. Students often conflate 'motion in a plane' with 'motion on a flat surface'; clarify that the plane here is a geometric concept, not necessarily a horizontal floor. The transition to circular motion in the following unit will build on the recognition that circular paths are the simplest two-dimensional case treated at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Exploring Velocity Direction in Uniform Circular Motion with a Marble
materials: Small circular ring or embroidery hoop (one per group)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of a circle showing the tangent direction at several points around the circumference

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a circle on the board and marks several points. Students predict: if an object is moving along this circle at point P, in which direction is it moving? They draw arrows at each marked point.

Students perform Activity 4.5 in groups: place a marble inside a ring on a smooth surface, spin it so it moves along the inner boundary, then lift the ring sharply mid-motion and observe the marble's path after release. Each group records the direction of motion after release relative to the position on the ring where they lifted it.

Groups share observations. Class consolidates: the marble always travels in a straight line tangent to the circle at the point of release. Teacher connects this to the board diagram — velocity direction is always along the tangent, perpendicular to the radius at that point.

Discussion: 'If velocity direction keeps changing, what does that imply about acceleration?' Students use the definition of acceleration (change in velocity / time) to reason that circular motion must involve acceleration even at constant speed.
Students write one sentence: 'In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but the object is accelerating because…' completing the sentence with their own reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The marble activity provides direct sensory evidence of the tangential velocity direction — students who observe the marble travel in a straight line after the ring is lifted can reason about direction from their own data. The central conceptual challenge is that 'acceleration' in physics means any change in velocity, including direction change at constant speed; this is a genuine shift from everyday language. Ask: 'If a car moves at a steady speedometer reading around a roundabout, is it accelerating?' to probe whether students have genuinely revised their concept.

periods.activity_title: Calculating Average Speed for One Revolution and Confirming Zero Displacement
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of a circle with radius R labelled, circumference formula 2πR, and displacement = 0 for one full revolution indicated by start and end at same point

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a circle with radius R on the board. Students identify: (a) the distance travelled in one revolution = circumference = 2πR; (b) the displacement after one revolution = 0, because start and end points coincide. The average velocity over one revolution is therefore also zero.

Teacher introduces Eq. 4.5: v_av = 2πR/T, where T is the time period. Units are verified (m s⁻¹). Students work through a numerical example: a stone on a string of radius 0.5 m completes one revolution in 2 s — find average speed.

Students work on the worksheet: three problems involving circles of different radii and time periods, requiring calculation of average speed, distance per revolution, and displacement per revolution. One problem asks for T given speed and radius.

Students form pairs and compare solutions, identifying any errors in applying the formula or confusing distance with displacement. Teacher addresses any systematic errors in a brief whole-class clarification.

Teacher poses the conceptual question: 'If average velocity is zero over one full revolution but average speed is not, what does this imply about the direction of motion?' Students answer individually in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that velocity direction is tangential in the previous unit, this unit formalises the quantitative relationships. Students frequently confuse distance (2πR) with displacement (0) for a full revolution; the circle diagram with identical start and end point is the most direct way to resolve this. Check that students can distinguish the cases: average speed over one revolution is non-zero and calculable, but average velocity over one revolution is zero — both are simultaneously true.

periods.activity_title: Distinguishing Physics Acceleration from Everyday Usage in Circular Motion
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram comparing: (a) object speeding up in a straight line — velocity direction constant, magnitude changing; (b) uniform circular motion — speed constant, direction changing

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents two scenarios on the board: a car accelerating on a straight highway, and a car going around a roundabout at constant speed. Students vote on which car is 'accelerating' in everyday language and in physics. Results are tallied and the discrepancy (if any) is noted.

Teacher draws the two board diagrams: straight-line acceleration (magnitude changes, direction fixed) vs. uniform circular motion (magnitude fixed, direction changes). Students use the definition a = Δv/Δt to reason about both: in both cases Δv ≠ 0, so acceleration exists in both cases.

Students write a structured comparison in their notebooks: two rows (straight-line non-uniform motion; uniform circular motion) against three columns (speed changes?, velocity direction changes?, is there acceleration?). They fill in the table and write a two-sentence summary of what distinguishes the physics definition of acceleration from the everyday sense.

Students share their summaries in pairs. The teacher leads a brief discussion connecting uniform circular motion to real-world idealised models: planetary orbits and vehicle turns as approximate cases.
Whole class constructs a single agreed definition: 'Acceleration in physics means… while in everyday language it often means only…' — recorded on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The everyday-vs-physics distinction around acceleration is one of the most durable misconceptions in mechanics, and this unit addresses it directly. Students who have computed slope on velocity-time graphs and derived a = Δv/Δt have the precise tool to reason about both cases; bring that definition to the fore explicitly. The comparison table is an effective scaffold because it separates the two components of velocity (magnitude and direction) and lets students apply the definition independently to each.

periods.activity_title: Integrating Displacement, Graphs, and Kinematic Equations in Novel Scenarios
periods.section_anchor: 4.1.2 Distance travelled and displacement / 4.2.3 Velocity-time graphs / 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
materials: Worksheet with three multi-part integration problems (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Velocity-time graph on board for one of the problems showing a combined constant-velocity and constant-acceleration phase

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents a composite motion scenario on the board: an object moves at constant velocity for a period, then decelerates to rest. A velocity-time graph is sketched (not labelled numerically). Students predict what the graph shape will look like and what quantities they could extract.

Students work individually on the worksheet: three multi-part problems each requiring (a) reading or sketching a velocity-time graph, (b) calculating displacement from area, and (c) using an appropriate kinematic equation to find a missing quantity. Problems involve displacement as a signed quantity, requiring attention to direction.
Students form groups of three, compare solutions, and produce a jointly agreed set of answers. Groups must identify which equation they used for part (c) and justify the choice.
Two groups present contrasting approaches (graph area vs. kinematic equation) for the same problem. Class discusses whether both give the same answer and why they should.
Students write one sentence connecting the two methods: 'The area under the velocity-time graph equals displacement because…'

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together displacement, velocity-time graph area, and kinematic equations — three representations of the same physical reality. Students often treat the graphical and algebraic methods as separate tools; the goal here is to build confidence that they are equivalent, so a discrepancy between them signals an error to be found and fixed. Watch for sign errors in displacement when an object decelerates to rest and students mistakenly continue computing motion beyond that point.

periods.activity_title: Cross-Checking Motion Representations: Sketch, Calculate, and Verify
periods.section_anchor: 4.2.2 Position-time graphs / 4.2.3 Velocity-time graphs / 4.3 Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration
materials: Worksheet with one rich multi-representation problem (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Teacher-drawn paired position-time and velocity-time graphs on board for the same motion scenario

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents a rich scenario: an object starts from rest, accelerates uniformly for a stated time, then moves at constant velocity for a further stated time. Students first predict what both the position-time and velocity-time graphs will look like before any calculation.

Students compute a table of (time, position) and (time, velocity) values using kinematic equations, then plot both graphs on graph paper. They check that the slope of the position-time graph during the constant-velocity phase matches the constant velocity value.

Students verify: (a) the slope of the velocity-time graph during the accelerating phase equals the stated acceleration; (b) the area under the velocity-time graph for both phases combined equals the total displacement from the position-time graph. They record any discrepancies and identify the source.
Pairs compare their completed graphs. Any discrepancy between the two students' graphs is used as a diagnostic: they identify whether the error was in calculation, scale, or plotting.
Students annotate their graphs: label the acceleration phase, constant-velocity phase, and mark where slope and area were used as verification tools.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to hold three representations — sketch prediction, calculated table, and plotted graph — simultaneously for the same motion, and to use them as mutual checks. The verification step (area equals displacement from position-time graph) is the highest-demand task; students who succeed have built a coherent multi-representational model of kinematic motion. A common issue is scale mismatch between the two graphs making visual comparison difficult; encourage students to use the same time scale on both x-axes.

periods.activity_title: Evaluating Real-World Motion Claims Using Circular Motion Concepts
periods.section_anchor: 4.4 Motion in a Plane / 4.4.1 Uniform circular motion
materials: Printed or board-written set of four real-world motion claims (teacher-prepared)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of a satellite orbit and a car on a roundabout, with tangent velocity direction indicated at two points each

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents four real-world claims on the board, e.g.: (a) 'A satellite at constant orbital speed is not accelerating'; (b) 'A car going around a circular track at 60 km/h has zero displacement after one full lap'; (c) 'A cyclist on a circular velodrome at constant speed has constant velocity'; (d) 'Increasing the radius of a circular path while keeping time period constant increases average speed.' Students read and privately mark each claim as true or false.

Students work individually to evaluate each claim using concepts from the chapter — displacement vs. distance, the definition of acceleration as any change in velocity including direction, and v_av = 2πR/T. They write a justification for each verdict referencing the specific concept used.
Students form groups of four, share their verdicts and justifications, and reach a group consensus on any disagreements. Groups prepare a one-sentence justification for each claim.
Each group presents one claim's verdict and justification. Class discusses any contested cases; the teacher uses the board diagrams to resolve directional arguments about velocity and acceleration.
Students individually write a two-sentence reflection: 'Before this chapter, I thought acceleration meant… Now I understand it means… because uniform circular motion shows that…'

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings together the chapter's two main domains — linear motion concepts (displacement, velocity, acceleration) and uniform circular motion — by asking students to apply them critically to real-world claims. The claim-evaluation format requires students to distinguish between speed and velocity, and between everyday and physics definitions of acceleration, in a single coherent activity. Students who write confident justifications for all four claims, including the radius-speed relationship in claim (d), have demonstrated integrated command of the chapter.

questions.question_text: An object is placed 4 m to the left of the origin O on a number line. Its position is recorded at two instants: first as −4 m, and then as −4 m again. Which of the following correctly describes the object's state?

options.label: A
options.text: The object is in motion because it has a negative position value.

options.label: B
options.text: The object is at rest because its position with respect to O has not changed.

options.label: C
options.text: The object is at rest only if the origin O has also not moved.

options.label: D
options.text: The object is in motion because it is located away from the origin.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates sign of position with evidence of motion; treats negative position as implying movement rather than reading the definition of motion as change in position over time.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a conditional about the origin moving — an irrelevant concern that shows the student has not internalised that the origin is fixed by definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Treats non-zero position as equivalent to motion; confuses 'distance from origin' with 'change in position over time'.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with signed number conventions may correctly reason about rest and motion if the question is re-posed with positions 0 m and 0 m — accepting verbal justification ('position did not change') alongside numerical reasoning.

questions.question_text: A ball is thrown vertically upward from ground level (position = 0 m). It rises to a height of 6 m, then falls back down to a height of 2 m above the ground. (a) Calculate the total distance travelled. (b) Calculate the displacement. (c) State whether the magnitude of displacement is greater than, equal to, or less than the distance travelled, and give a reason.
expected_elements: Distance travelled = 6 m (upward) + 4 m (downward from 6 m to 2 m) = 10 m
Displacement = final position − initial position = 2 m − 0 m = +2 m (upward)
Magnitude of displacement (2 m) is less than distance travelled (10 m) because the ball reversed direction, so the path length exceeds the net positional change

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find algebraic notation difficult may draw the number line path and annotate segment lengths; accept this as equivalent reasoning for parts (a) and (b) provided the numerical values and reasoning in (c) are present.

questions.question_text: A runner starts at position 0 m, runs to +80 m in 20 s, then turns and runs back to +20 m in 15 s. Taking the positive direction as away from the start: (a) Calculate the average speed for the entire journey. (b) Calculate the average velocity for the entire journey. (c) Explain in one sentence why average speed and average velocity differ here.
expected_elements: Total distance = 80 m + 60 m = 140 m; total time = 35 s; average speed = 140/35 = 4 m s⁻¹
Displacement = 20 m − 0 m = +20 m; average velocity = 20/35 ≈ +0.57 m s⁻¹
Average speed and average velocity differ because the runner reversed direction, so total path length (140 m) exceeds the magnitude of net displacement (20 m)

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about sign conventions may narrate the journey verbally before writing equations; credit a correct unsigned speed and a separately computed net-displacement velocity even if sign labelling is incomplete, provided the conceptual explanation in (c) is accurate.

questions.question_text: A bus moving in the positive direction has a velocity of +18 m s⁻¹ at one instant and +10 m s⁻¹ eight seconds later. Which statement correctly describes its average acceleration?

options.label: A
options.text: Average acceleration = +1 m s⁻², in the positive direction, because the bus is still moving forward.

options.label: B
options.text: Average acceleration = −1 m s⁻², opposite to the direction of velocity, because the speed is decreasing.

options.label: C
options.text: Average acceleration = −8 m s⁻², because we subtract the time from the initial velocity.

options.label: D
options.text: Average acceleration = 0, because the bus never changes direction.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Computes the correct magnitude (8/8 = 1) but assigns a positive sign — confusing the direction of motion with the sign of acceleration; does not recognise that decreasing speed means acceleration opposes velocity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies a nonsensical operation (subtracting time from velocity), revealing a procedural misunderstanding of the formula for acceleration.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Equates change in direction with acceleration and concludes zero acceleration whenever direction is constant — a core misconception the section directly addresses.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students may compute the numerical value correctly even if they struggle with sign interpretation; partial credit or verbal follow-up ('Is the bus speeding up or slowing down?') can separate procedural from conceptual understanding.

questions.question_text: Refer to the table provided. (a) On graph paper, draw a position-time graph for this data: label both axes with the quantity and unit, choose a scale that spreads the points across the paper, plot all five points, and connect them. (b) Describe the shape of the graph and state what it tells you about the type of motion. (c) Suppose a second object had position values of 0, 3, 12, 27, 48 m at the same time instants. Sketch (without re-plotting) what that graph would look like and explain the difference in shape.
expected_elements: Graph with time on X-axis (s) and position on Y-axis (m), a chosen scale that places points across the paper, all five points correctly plotted, and a straight line connecting them
Shape is a straight line; this indicates constant velocity / uniform motion — equal distances covered in equal time intervals
Second data set (0, 3, 12, 27, 48 m) increases non-uniformly, so the graph would curve upward; this indicates non-uniform motion / changing (increasing) velocity

SCR.inclusivity: Students who have difficulty drawing the graph on plain paper may be offered pre-labelled axes; the cognitive demand (scale selection, shape interpretation, curve comparison) remains the same. Verbal explanation of the curve shape for part (c) is acceptable in place of a sketch.

questions.visual_stimulus: Description: A position-time graph shows two straight lines from the origin. Line P reaches position 40 m at time 8 s. Line Q reaches position 40 m at time 5 s.
questions.question_text: The figure described shows two straight-line position-time graphs for objects P and Q, both starting from the origin. (a) Using the triangle method (choose two points, draw vertical and horizontal construction lines, compute rise/run), calculate the average velocity of each object. (b) State which object has greater velocity and explain how the slope of the line shows this. (c) What would a horizontal line on this graph indicate about an object's motion?
expected_elements: Velocity of P = (40 − 0)/(8 − 0) = 5 m s⁻¹; velocity of Q = (40 − 0)/(5 − 0) = 8 m s⁻¹ (triangle construction described with rise = change in position, run = change in time)
Object Q has greater velocity; steeper slope (greater rise for the same run, or same rise for less run) corresponds to higher velocity
A horizontal line indicates the position does not change over time — the object is at rest

SCR.inclusivity: Students who invert slope (run/rise) may still demonstrate understanding of the steeper-line comparison in part (b); accept the comparison reasoning as a separate credit component. Students may describe the triangle construction verbally if they cannot sketch it.

questions.question_text: Refer to the table provided. It describes an object's motion in two phases: Phase 1 from t = 0 s to t = 3 s (velocity increases uniformly from 4 m s⁻¹ to 10 m s⁻¹), and Phase 2 from t = 3 s to t = 7 s (velocity stays constant at 10 m s⁻¹). (a) Calculate the acceleration during Phase 1. (b) Calculate the displacement during Phase 1 using the trapezoid area method. (c) Calculate the displacement during Phase 2. (d) State the total displacement over both phases.
expected_elements: Phase 1 displacement = area of trapezoid = ½ × (4 + 10) × 3 = ½ × 14 × 3 = 21 m
Phase 2 displacement = area of rectangle = 10 × 4 = 40 m

SCR.inclusivity: Students who treat Phase 1 as a rectangle (using only one velocity value) may still demonstrate correct area understanding for Phase 2; award credit for parts that are independently correct. Students who write the correct formula for trapezoid area but apply it with an arithmetic error should receive method credit.

questions.question_text: A car is travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ when the driver applies the brakes, producing a constant deceleration of 4 m s⁻². A second identical car is travelling at 40 m s⁻¹ under the same braking deceleration. (a) Calculate the stopping distance for each car using an appropriate kinematic equation. (b) Compare the stopping distances and explain the mathematical relationship between initial speed and stopping distance. (c) A road safety engineer claims: 'Doubling the speed limit on a road does not simply double the required stopping distance — it is far more dangerous than that.' Evaluate this claim using your calculations and the relevant kinematic equation, stating clearly which equation you used and why.
look_for: Correct selection of v² = u² + 2as with v = 0, a = −4 m s⁻² and correct manipulation to find s
Recognition that stopping distance quadruples when speed doubles (because s ∝ u²)
Evaluation of the engineer's claim: doubling speed quadruples stopping distance, not doubles it — the relationship is quadratic, not linear, making higher speeds disproportionately more dangerous
Explicit identification of v² = u² + 2as as the relevant equation and a statement that t is absent from this scenario

ECR.inclusivity: Students who correctly calculate both stopping distances but struggle to articulate the proportionality argument algebraically may express the quadratic relationship numerically (50 m vs. 200 m, ratio of 4) — accept numerical evidence as equivalent to algebraic derivation for the comparison. Students who cannot evaluate the engineer's claim in full may receive partial credit for the calculation parts.

questions.question_text: Which of the following motions requires two coordinates to fully describe the object's position at every instant?

options.label: A
options.text: A ball rolling along a straight corridor.

options.label: B
options.text: A stone dropped vertically from a building.

options.label: C
options.text: A satellite moving in a circular orbit around Earth.

options.label: D
options.text: A train moving along a straight track at constant speed.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Selects a one-dimensional example; student may have read 'motion' without attending to whether the path is straight or curved, or may not have connected 'two coordinates' to a curved path.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selects a one-dimensional vertical fall; student may associate 'plane' with any two-dimensional physical space rather than with the geometry of the path itself.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selects another one-dimensional example; the distractor surfaces students who interpret 'constant speed' as the defining feature of two-dimensional motion rather than the path geometry.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who select C correctly but struggle to explain why may articulate the reasoning orally — 'you need to know both how far across and how far up the orbit the satellite is' — which is acceptable as a demonstration of the same understanding.

competency.competency_text: Describe and analyse motion in one dimension and uniform circular motion by applying displacement, velocity, and acceleration, and by reading, plotting, and interpreting position-time and velocity-time graphs and kinematic equations.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Radius (m) | Time for one revolution (s)
Athletic track runner | 50 | 62.8
Model satellite orbit | 8000000 | 5655
questions.task: You are given data for two objects in uniform circular motion in the table provided. Use the data and your knowledge of uniform circular motion to complete the following tasks.
questions.scaffold:
1. For each object, calculate the average speed over one complete revolution using v_av = 2πR/T. Show all working and state the unit of your answer.
2. For each object, state the displacement after exactly one complete revolution. Justify your answer in one sentence.
3. At the moment the runner completes a quarter of the track (one quarter revolution from the start), draw a circle and mark: (a) the runner's position, (b) the direction of velocity at that point as an arrow, and (c) the direction from the centre to the runner (the radius direction). Label your diagram.
4. A classmate says: 'The runner cannot be accelerating because the speedometer never changes.' Using the physics definition of acceleration and your diagram from Task 3, write a response of 3–4 sentences that evaluates this claim and explains whether it is correct or incorrect.
format_of_output: Numerical calculations with working shown for Task 1

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation (provided table) combined with diagram completion and annotation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Uniform circular motion integrates quantitative calculation (v_av = 2πR/T), conceptual understanding (zero displacement per revolution), spatial reasoning (tangent direction diagram), and evaluative argumentation (acceleration despite constant speed) — no single question type can test all four operations simultaneously; an open task with a scaffolded sequence is the most natural vehicle.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether students can move fluently between quantitative application of the circular motion formula, conceptual reasoning about displacement, diagrammatic representation of velocity direction, and evaluative argument using the physics definition of acceleration.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Task 1 is purely computational and accessible to all; Task 2 requires conceptual application of the displacement definition; Task 3 is spatial and diagnostic for understanding tangential direction; Task 4 is the evaluative core and the most demanding — it requires students to use the physics definition of acceleration (any change in velocity including direction) to refute the everyday-language claim.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correct use of 2πR/T with units; explicit statement that displacement = 0 because start and end positions are identical; arrow perpendicular to the radius in the diagram; Task 4 explicitly states that velocity direction changes continuously and applies a = Δv/Δt to argue acceleration exists. Weak responses: use circumference as displacement; draw velocity arrow along the radius; Task 4 only restates the claim without using the acceleration definition.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the diagram may describe the velocity direction verbally ('the runner moves sideways to the line joining them to the centre') — accept this as equivalent spatial reasoning. For Task 1, students who recall the formula but need to verify the value of π may approximate it as 3.14; credit the method.
